sources.title: NCBI Bookshelf: The Innate and Adaptive Immune Systems

questions.question: A 17-year-old has a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. HIV testing is negative and immunoglobulin levels are normal. Which immune defect is most strongly suggested?
choices: Deficiency of terminal complement components that form the membrane attack complex
Isolated absence of IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation
Excessive production of C3b with increased opsonization
Loss of thymic negative selection alone
rationales: Recurrent Neisseria infection is classically associated with deficiency of C5 through C9 and impaired membrane attack complex formation.
IgE-mediated mast-cell function is not the principal defense explaining this pattern.
Increased C3b would enhance rather than impair opsonization.
T-cell selection defects can cause immune disease but are not the classic isolated association with recurrent Neisseria.
questions.explanation: The organism pattern can localize an immune defect. Recurrent invasive Neisseria should prompt evaluation of terminal complement function.

questions.question: A child with severe C3 deficiency develops recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria. Which lost complement function most directly explains the susceptibility?
choices: C3b-mediated opsonization that facilitates phagocytic recognition
C9-mediated T-cell receptor rearrangement
IgA class switching in mucosal plasma cells
Natural-killer-cell recognition of absent MHC I
rationales: C3b coats microbes and improves recognition by complement receptors on phagocytes; its loss impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms.
C9 contributes to the membrane attack complex, not T-cell receptor rearrangement.
Immunoglobulin class switching is an adaptive B-cell process.
Natural killer recognition is distinct from C3-mediated opsonization.
questions.explanation: C3 occupies a central position in complement activation, linking amplification, opsonization, inflammation, and downstream terminal-pathway activity.

questions.question: A patient receiving chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 300/µL and an oral temperature of 38.4°C. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
choices: Possible neutropenic infection requiring urgent evaluation because inflammation may be muted despite severe disease
A reassuring fever because neutrophils are required to generate temperature elevation
Likely isolated adaptive-memory activation appropriate for routine follow-up
Evidence that complement alone will reliably contain bacterial invasion
rationales: Profound neutropenia markedly increases infection risk; local inflammatory findings may be subtle, so fever warrants urgent assessment.
Fever can occur through cytokine pathways even when neutrophil counts are low.
The presentation is not safely attributed to benign memory-cell activation.
Complement cannot compensate reliably for severe loss of cellular innate defense.
questions.explanation: Immune status changes the meaning of clinical findings. A small or nonspecific sign can carry greater urgency in a profoundly neutropenic patient.

questions.question: Airway macrophages recognize conserved bacterial motifs before a pathogen-specific antibody response has developed. Which receptor concept best explains this rapid recognition?
choices: Germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors identify shared pathogen-associated molecular patterns
Somatically rearranged B-cell receptors are expressed on every macrophage
MHC molecules directly generate pathogen-specific antibodies
Complement proteins permanently memorize each prior bacterial strain
rationales: Innate pattern-recognition receptors detect conserved microbial or damage-associated patterns without prior exposure.
Somatically rearranged antigen receptors characterize lymphocytes, not every macrophage.
MHC presents peptides to T cells but does not generate antibodies.
Complement lacks antigen-specific memory.
questions.explanation: Innate immunity trades receptor diversity for speed: conserved receptors trigger inflammation while adaptive specificity develops.

questions.question: A child has recurrent deep abscesses caused by catalase-positive organisms. Neutrophil count is normal, but oxidative-burst testing is abnormal. Which defect best fits?
choices: Impaired NADPH oxidase activity prevents effective generation of microbicidal reactive oxygen species
Absent terminal complement selectively prevents antibody production
Excess histamine prevents neutrophil chemotaxis in every tissue
Failure of B-cell class switching eliminates phagocytosis
rationales: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective phagocyte NADPH oxidase and impaired respiratory burst killing.
Terminal complement deficiency is associated especially with Neisseria and does not explain abnormal oxidative-burst testing.
Histamine excess is not the unifying inherited defect.
Antibody class switching is adaptive and does not directly generate the phagocyte respiratory burst.
questions.explanation: Normal cell numbers do not guarantee normal cell function. Functional testing can reveal a phagocyte killing defect.

questions.question: An adult with prior splenectomy presents with abrupt fever, rigors, and confusion. Which physiologic concern should drive disposition?
choices: Loss of splenic filtration and opsonized-organism clearance increases risk of rapidly progressive infection with encapsulated bacteria
Loss of the spleen prevents all viral replication but increases seasonal allergy symptoms
Splenectomy eliminates complement production and therefore makes fever impossible
The spleen is needed only for platelet storage, so routine outpatient follow-up is sufficient
rationales: The spleen helps clear opsonized encapsulated organisms; postsplenectomy sepsis can progress rapidly and demands urgent evaluation.
Splenectomy does not prevent viral replication.
Most complement proteins are produced mainly by the liver, and fever remains possible.
The spleen has important immune as well as hematologic functions.
questions.explanation: The same fever carries different risk in an asplenic patient. Host-defense context should influence urgency before an organism is known.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent episodes of nonpruritic lip and tongue swelling without urticaria. A parent has similar episodes. Antihistamines have provided little benefit. Which pathway is most likely?
choices: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema related to deficient or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor
IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells
C3b excess causing immune-complex deposition
CD8 T-cell destruction of salivary glands
rationales: Hereditary angioedema is commonly bradykinin mediated, often familial, lacks urticaria, and responds poorly to antihistamines.
Histamine-mediated angioedema more often includes urticaria or pruritus and may respond to antihistamines.
C3b excess does not explain the episodic familial pattern.
Cytotoxic injury to salivary glands would not produce this acute swelling syndrome.
questions.explanation: Distinguishing bradykinin- from histamine-mediated angioedema matters, but any tongue or airway involvement requires immediate airway-focused assessment.

questions.question: A patient with sepsis has persistent hypotension, mottled skin, rising lactate, and altered mentation despite initial treatment. Which statement best characterizes the innate immune contribution?
choices: A dysregulated host response can injure endothelium, disrupt microcirculation, activate coagulation, and impair organs
Innate activation remains strictly localized and cannot affect distant organs
Complement and cytokines only improve perfusion and never contribute to tissue injury
Organ dysfunction proves that no pathogen-recognition signaling occurred
rationales: Systemic innate signaling can become dysregulated, contributing to endothelial leak, vasodilation, coagulation abnormalities, and organ injury.
Severe infection can generate systemic rather than only localized effects.
Protective mediators can become harmful when excessive or poorly regulated.
Organ dysfunction may occur precisely because host-response pathways are intensely activated and dysregulated.
questions.explanation: Sepsis is not simply pathogen burden; the host response and microcirculatory consequences help determine organ dysfunction and trajectory.

questions.question: A transformed cell markedly reduces surface MHC class I expression. Which innate immune cell is best positioned to recognize this missing-self signal?
choices: Natural killer cell
Neutrophil
Eosinophil
Plasma cell
rationales: Natural killer cells integrate activating and inhibitory signals and can target cells with reduced MHC I expression.
Neutrophils are rapid phagocytes but are not specialized for missing-self recognition.
Eosinophils are prominent in selected parasitic and allergic responses.
Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibody.
questions.explanation: Natural killer cells provide rapid surveillance without a rearranged antigen-specific receptor and complement cytotoxic T-cell defenses.

questions.question: During complement activation, which fragment is especially important for neutrophil chemotaxis and amplification of inflammation?
choices: C5a
C3b
C9
C1 inhibitor
rationales: C5a is a potent anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant that recruits and activates neutrophils.
C3b is best known for opsonization and participation in convertases.
C9 polymerizes in the membrane attack complex.
C1 inhibitor limits early classical-pathway and contact-system activation rather than serving as a chemoattractant.
questions.explanation: Complement fragments have distinct functions: C3b opsonizes, C5a recruits and activates inflammatory cells, and C5b–C9 forms the membrane attack complex.
